q: A team must answer questions over internal policies that change weekly. Which first lever is most appropriate?
options: Fine-tune a model on the policies each week
Retrieval over an index re-built when policies change
why: Retrieval handles changing private knowledge cheaply and with citations. Weekly fine-tuning is slow, costly and does not reliably inject facts.

q: Your p95 latency target is 2 s for a chat feature. Which requirement-gathering outcome matters most for architecture?
options: The latency budget and its binding effect on model size and call count
why: A hard latency budget limits sequential calls, context size and model choice. It must be known before choosing components.

q: Which statement about fine-tuning is the most accurate?
options: It is the best way to add fresh facts
It removes the need for evals
It is always cheaper than prompting
It mainly changes behaviour, style or distils skill into a smaller model
why: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour and format; facts are better supplied by retrieval or tools. It needs data and evals.

q: An LLM feature costs too much. 85% of requests are simple classification-like asks. Best first move?
options: Switch everything to the largest model
Route simple requests to a smaller model and escalate the rest
Add a second call to verify every answer
why: Routing exploits the traffic skew for a large blended saving. Verifying every answer with another call adds cost.

q: Why build an evaluation set before adding components to a baseline?
options: It lets you attribute quality changes to each component and stop when criteria are met
why: Without a fixed metric you cannot tell whether a reranker or agent helped. Evals turn design into measured decisions.

q: A task has an unknown number of lookups depending on earlier results. Which approach fits?
options: A tool-using loop (agent) with step and cost limits
why: Data-dependent steps are the legitimate use of an agent loop, but with caps on steps, time and spend.

q: Which source is best for the current status of a customer's order?
options: A tool call to the order API
why: Exact, changing, per-user data should come from the authoritative system via a tool, not from memory or stale caches.

q: A query containing an error code 'E4021' fails in dense search. Most direct improvement?
options: Add keyword (BM25) retrieval and fuse results
why: Exact tokens are the strength of lexical search. Hybrid retrieval with fusion covers both exact and semantic queries.

q: Where should per-user document permissions be enforced in a RAG system?
why: The model must not receive unauthorised text. Filtering at retrieval prevents leakage; prompt instructions are not a security boundary.

q: A 4k-token policy is needed on every request of a high-volume bot. Reasonable design?
options: Keep it in a cached prompt prefix
Ask the user to paste it
why: Small, always-relevant content suits holding in context, and caching lowers repeated cost. Retrieval risks missing it.

q: Why log which passages were included in each prompt?
options: To debug whether wrong answers come from retrieval, ranking, budget or generation
why: Without logged context you cannot tell which stage failed. It also supports audits and citations.

q: Reciprocal rank fusion is useful because it:
options: Requires calibrated scores from each retriever
Merges ranked lists using ranks, avoiding score calibration
why: RRF sums 1/(k+rank) across lists, so BM25 and vector scores on different scales can be combined directly.

q: What is the primary benefit of a model gateway for provider deprecations?
options: It removes the need for evals
Model selection and parameters change in one place and can be rolled out gradually
why: Centralised configuration turns a many-service code change into one controlled migration. Evals are still required.

q: A cascade is most cost-effective when:
options: The first-stage accept rate is high and the check is well calibrated
The cheap model is slower than the large one
why: Savings come from avoiding the expensive call on most traffic. Frequent escalation means paying both calls.

q: For a high-stakes legal-advice route, what fallback policy is most defensible?
options: Silently switch to any cheap model
Use a pre-qualified equivalent, or fail visibly/queue rather than silently degrade
why: High-risk routes need quality guarantees; unqualified silent fallbacks risk harm. Visible failure or a validated backup is safer.

q: Which is a routing signal rather than a cascade signal?
options: The cheap model's answer failing validation
Request type and user plan known before any model call
why: Routing happens before generation from request features; the others depend on a produced answer.

q: Why track tokens and cost per feature at the gateway?
options: For attribution, budgets, anomaly detection and capacity planning
why: Per-feature attribution reveals runaway loops and enables chargeback and limits.

q: A team's global rate limit lets one batch job starve interactive chat. Best fix?
options: Separate per-feature quotas and priority for interactive traffic
why: Per-feature limits and priorities isolate workloads; simply raising quota just moves the contention.

q: A trace shows decode time is 80% of a 5 s response. Which change is most impactful?
options: Shorter outputs or a faster model, plus streaming for perceived speed
why: Decode dominates, so output length and model speed matter; the vector index is a small share.

q: What is the effect of running three independent 400 ms lookups in parallel?
options: Latency is about 400 ms but cost is not reduced
why: Parallelism takes the max not the sum. It does not reduce the work done, so cost is unchanged.

q: Why is streaming risky for a route that must pass a safety check before display?
options: Unsafe text could be shown before the check completes
why: The check needs the content; streaming shows tokens early. Buffer, moderate chunks, or avoid streaming on that route.

q: Which task is least suited to a small model without further work?
options: Open-ended multi-step reasoning over a long contract
why: Complex long-context reasoning is where small models typically fall short; the others are narrow and well-specified.

q: A batch of nightly enrichment jobs delays interactive requests on shared GPUs. Best fix?
options: Separate pools or priorities for interactive and batch work
why: Isolation and priority protect interactive SLOs; mixing workloads lets long batch work cause queueing.

q: What primarily limits concurrent sequences on a self-hosted GPU?
options: Memory for weights plus the KV cache
why: After weights are loaded, the KV cache per sequence grows with context length and bounds concurrency.

q: You must cut TTFT for a RAG bot sending 12k tokens each call. First options?
options: Reduce and rerank context, cache the stable prefix
why: Prefill grows with input tokens; trimming context and caching prefixes directly reduce TTFT.

q: Which cache reuses computation for an identical prompt prefix at the provider?
why: Prompt/prefix caching reuses attention state for repeated prefixes; it requires stable leading content.

q: Which response is least safe to cache?
options: A generic FAQ answer that passed validation
why: Balance is live and personal state; caching it yields stale or leaked data.

q: What does lowering the semantic-cache threshold generally do?
options: Raises hit rate and the risk of wrong matches
why: A looser similarity requirement matches more queries, including ones that only look similar but differ in intent.

q: Prompt cache hit rate is poor. The prompt begins with the current time. Fix?
options: Move the timestamp after the stable prefix
why: Any difference early in the prompt breaks prefix reuse; put stable content first and variable content last.

q: Which keying practice prevents cross-user leaks in a response cache?
options: Include tenant/user scope and permission context in the key
why: Answers that depend on identity or permissions must be keyed by that scope, or not cached.

q: Best way to detect a semantic cache returning wrong answers?
options: Sample hits and judge correctness; run a no-cache holdout
why: Correctness of hits must be audited; hit rate rewards wrong hits too.

q: Which approach to retrying a failing LLM provider is most appropriate?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop
Exponential backoff with jitter, capped attempts and a circuit breaker
why: Backoff with jitter avoids retry storms; capping and a breaker prevent amplifying load on a degraded provider.

q: Where should enforcement of 'human approval before refund' live?
options: In the tool executor that rejects calls lacking a bound approval
why: Prompts can be bypassed; the executor must deterministically refuse without a valid approval.

q: The LLM API is down. Which response best shows graceful degradation?
options: Return cached or retrieved help content, state limits, and offer human handoff
Retry for 5 minutes with the user waiting
why: Partial functionality with transparency preserves value and safety versus a hard failure or fabricated answer.

q: Which is a guardrail at the action boundary?
options: Validating tool arguments, allow-lists and spend limits before executing
why: The action boundary sits between model decisions and side effects, where arguments and privileges are enforced.

q: An SLO set only on uptime misses what?
options: Quality, latency and safety regressions while the service stays up
why: AI systems degrade silently; quality and safety need their own measurable targets.

q: A timeout is missing and a slow provider exhausts server threads. Best fix?
options: Per-call and overall deadlines, bounded concurrency and a circuit breaker
why: Deadlines and breakers bound resource use during a downstream slowdown; more threads just delays exhaustion.

q: Why measure guardrail precision and recall?
options: False positives block good users and false negatives let harm pass; both need tuning
why: A guardrail is a classifier with error trade-offs; without metrics you cannot tune it.

q: In 'model proposes, code disposes', who enforces refund limits?
options: Code that validates the proposed action against policy
why: Policy enforcement belongs in deterministic code; the model only proposes a structured intent.

q: A job takes ~8 minutes and involves many LLM calls. Best execution model?
options: Durable workflow with checkpointed steps and status updates
Browser polling a long-lived function with no state
why: Long tasks need persisted state, retries and resumability, not a request that can time out.

q: Which is the least agentic design that could solve 'retrieve, answer with citations, validate'?
options: A fixed pipeline with one generation call
why: The steps are known in advance, so a fixed workflow is simpler, cheaper and more reliable.

q: Ten dependent steps each 95% reliable give roughly what end-to-end success?
why: 0.95 to the power ten is about 0.60; compounding error is why long agent chains need validation.

q: Main benefit of separating ingestion from the serving path?
options: Heavy offline work does not consume request-time capacity and can scale independently
why: Offline pipelines are throughput-oriented and tolerant of delay; coupling them with serving hurts latency.

q: Which step should typically be deterministic code rather than an LLM call?
options: Checking a user's permission to view an order
why: Authorisation must be exact, auditable and testable, so it is not delegated to a probabilistic model.

q: Which change best attributes a quality regression to a cause?
options: Versioning prompts, models and index configs on each trace and comparing per-version metrics
why: Version stamps on traces let you slice quality by what changed; bundling changes destroys attribution.

q: Implicit feedback example:
options: User rephrases the same question immediately after an answer
why: Behavioural signals such as rewording the same ask suggest the first answer failed; they are noisy but abundant.

q: A single failing production case is fixed by editing the prompt. What must you do next?
options: Add it as a regression case and run the full eval set
why: The case should persist as a test, and the full set checks the edit did not break other behaviour.

q: Uptime is 100% yet users report wrong answers. Which monitoring is missing?
options: Sampled quality and groundedness scoring plus feedback signals
why: Silent quality failures do not raise errors; they require evals on sampled traffic and feedback.

q: Why calibrate an LLM judge against human labels?
options: To ensure its scores correlate with human judgement before trusting trends
why: An uncalibrated judge may be biased or inconsistent, making dashboards misleading.

q: Best rollout method for a new retrieval configuration?
options: Shadow or canary on a small share with automatic rollback metrics
why: Gradual exposure with thresholds limits blast radius while measuring real-world effect.

q: A support copilot quotes an outdated refund policy after an update. Most direct architectural fix?
options: Event-driven re-indexing with version metadata and cache invalidation
why: Staleness is an ingestion and cache problem; event-driven updates and invalidation by document version address it directly.

q: Which statement about citations in a support copilot is most correct?
options: Verify that the cited passage actually supports the claim
Checking that the cited id exists is enough
why: A real id can still be irrelevant or contradict the claim, so support must be checked.

q: Which request should NOT be served from a shared response cache?
options: How do I change my display name
Where is my order, for a specific customer
why: Order status is personal and live; it would be stale or leak across users.

q: A coding agent must run a repo's test suite. What is the key safety control?
options: An ephemeral sandbox with restricted filesystem, default-deny network and resource limits
why: Repository code is untrusted; isolation and limits contain damage and exfiltration.

q: For inline code completion, which model approach fits best?
options: Largest reasoning model with long deliberation
Small, fast code model with short context and cancellation
why: Completion is latency-critical and very frequent; small fast models are the right trade-off.

q: Why store raw fetched pages outside the prompt in a research agent?
options: To keep context small while enabling verified citations and later synthesis
why: An evidence store lets the agent pass compact notes with ids yet re-verify quotes and cite accurately.

q: A research run is killed by a deploy after 20 minutes. Best prevention?
options: Durable workflow with checkpointed idempotent steps
why: Persisted per-step state lets workers resume after restarts instead of losing the run.

q: In a design interview you present a deep research agent with many components. What most improves your answer?
options: Linking each component to a requirement and stating the trade-off and alternative
why: Interviewers score reasoning: choices justified by requirements, numbers, trade-offs and rejected alternatives.

q: A support bot escalates 1% of chats yet CSAT drops with confident wrong answers. First action?
options: Audit non-escalated samples and tighten confidence and risk triggers
why: Missed escalations are the likely cause; sampling non-escalated conversations measures and tunes the thresholds.

q: You are choosing a baseline before adding agents. What belongs in that baseline first?
options: The smallest system that meets the written requirements, plus an eval set that can reject extra parts
Every vendor tool in one diagram
why: A measured baseline is how you prove each added box helped. Starting with agents hides cost and latency.

q: A design interview asks what you would drop if the deadline moved a week left. Weak answer?
options: Cut the reranker and keep hybrid retrieval plus citations
Keep the eval gate and drop a second model route
Drop evaluation, monitoring and rollback so the demo looks complete
Ship FAQ cache first and add the agent later
why: Cuts should drop optional quality layers, not the proof you can operate the system. Demos without evals are not designs.

q: Policy pages change weekly; order status changes per request. How should knowledge be split?
options: Fine-tune both into the model weekly
Index policies with a freshness SLA; fetch order status through a tool at request time
Put both only in the system prompt
why: Slow-changing shared text is a retrieval problem. Live per-user facts belong in the source system via a tool.

q: A knowledge SLA says 'indexed within 15 minutes of publish'. What must you monitor?
options: Ingest lag, failed documents, and answers citing superseded versions
why: A freshness SLA is a pipeline metric plus user-visible staleness. Model internals do not prove the contract.

q: Why put auth, quotas and model ids on a gateway instead of in each feature?
options: One place can rotate keys, enforce per-feature budgets, and change models without a fleet-wide rewrite
It removes the need for tracing
why: Central policy is how you survive deprecations and noisy-neighbour jobs. Evals and traces still sit beside it.

q: A cascade's cheap model accepts 40% of traffic and the rest pay both calls. What should you do?
options: Retune the accept rule or skip the cascade; you are paying two calls most of the time
Raise temperature on the cheap model
why: Cascades pay off only when the first stage accepts most traffic with a calibrated check. 40% means double spend.

q: Users complain the bot feels slow even though total latency is 1.8 s. What often fixes perceived latency first?
options: Streaming tokens after a safe first chunk, plus a shorter first sentence
why: Time-to-first-token is what people feel. Streaming a checked prefix beats a silent 1.8 s wait.

q: A RAG call spends 70% of time in prefill on a 16k prompt. Best first cut?
options: Trim and rerank context, cache the stable prefix, drop unused tools from the schema
why: Prefill scales with input tokens. Smaller prompts and prefix cache attack the actual bottleneck.

q: A semantic cache keys only on the last user sentence. Two tenants ask similar questions. What leaks?
options: Nothing if cosine similarity is high
Tenant A's answer or documents to tenant B
why: Similarity without tenant and permission in the key is a cross-tenant leak. Never key personal answers on text alone.

q: When should you refuse to cache a response even if the query looks repeated?
options: When the answer is a public FAQ
When the prompt prefix is stable
When the answer depends on live account state or a write action
why: Live and side-effecting answers go stale or replay a write. Cache only validated, scoped, read-only results.

q: Which SLO is actually pageable for an LLM route?
options: Availability, p95 latency, error rate, and a quality canary — each with an owner and a runbook
A weekly vibe check in chat
why: Pages need a number, a threshold and a person. Soft quality slogans and raw GPU stats do not tell you to wake someone.

q: The primary model is down. For a medical-advice route, which fallback is defensible?
options: Silently switch to an untested cheap model
Retry forever in the user request
Serve a pre-qualified backup or a visible 'unavailable, escalate to a clinician' path
Return a cached answer from another patient
why: High-stakes routes fail closed or to a known-good path. Silent degrade and cross-user cache are harm.

q: A ticket triage flow is a fixed five-step flowchart. Why avoid an open agent loop?
options: A DAG or workflow is cheaper, testable and bounded; an agent adds unneeded branching
why: Known graphs belong in orchestration. Agents are for data-dependent unknown steps, and they cost latency and evals.

q: Two pipeline steps can run independently after ingest. What do you gain by running them in parallel?
options: Wall-clock latency near the slower step, not the sum
why: Parallelism cuts latency to the max of independent work. It does not reduce tokens or fix quality.

q: A production failure is fixed in a prompt. What else must happen for it to stay fixed?
options: Turn it into a versioned eval case and add it to the weekly improve loop
why: Incidents become regressions unless they are fixtures. Versioned evals and a weekly loop keep the fix honest.

q: Thumbs-down is rare but users rewrite the bot's draft a lot. What signal are you missing?
options: Implicit feedback: edits, retries, abandon, and copy-without-send
why: Explicit ratings under-sample pain. Behavioural edits tell you which answers were unusable.

q: On the whiteboard, a coding assistant must edit a 2M-line repo. Which design do you defend first?
options: Stuff the whole repo into one context window
Repo retrieval plus a sandboxed executor, with the model proposing diffs not owning the workspace
why: Large codebases are retrieval plus isolated execution. Full-repo context and production access are unsafe and do not scale.

q: A one-pager a staff engineer would sign is missing a cut list and rollback. Why reject it?
options: Without cuts and rollback the design cannot shrink or recover, so it is a demo script not an operable system
why: Staff sign-off needs requirements, risks, eval, cost, rollback and what you would drop. Pretty diagrams are not enough.
